category_info.light_need: Medium to bright indirect light; avoid prolonged harsh direct sunlight
category_info.humidity: Moderate to high humidity (50-70% preferred); tolerates standard household humidity
category_info.soil_mix: Chunky, well-draining aroid mix containing peat or coco coir, perlite, orchid bark, and pumice
category_info.fertilizer: Balanced liquid houseplant fertilizer diluted to half strength monthly during active spring and summer growth
category_info.repotting: Every 1-2 years during spring when roots become pot-bound or circle the container
category_info.toxicity_to_pets: Toxic to cats and dogs if ingested due to insoluble calcium oxalate crystals

observations.location: Older and middle leaves, covering nearly the entire leaf lamina
observations.evidence: Multiple large fenestrated leaves and a smaller lower leaf are bright yellow, with only residual light green along select vein sectors
A smaller, lower leaf beneath the large fenestrated leaf has turned completely pale yellow

observations.location: Other mature leaves lower and adjacent on the plant
observations.evidence: Green, fenestrated leaves remain relatively vibrant green in the lower-right area

possible_causes.name: Overwatering and potential root rot
possible_causes.reason: Sudden, widespread uniform yellowing across multiple mature leaves in Monstera is most commonly caused by saturated soil suffocating the root system, preventing water and oxygen transport.

possible_causes.name: Severe nitrogen deficiency or nutrient depletion
possible_causes.reason: Nitrogen is a mobile nutrient, so plants will withdraw nitrogen from older foliage to sustain new growth, causing uniform yellowing from older leaves upwards.

possible_causes.name: Acclimation or temperature shock
possible_causes.reason: Exposure to cold drafts, rapid environmental changes, or prolonged severe underwatering followed by heavy flooding can trigger rapid chlorosis and shedding of older leaves.

recommended_actions.action: Check soil moisture and root health
recommended_actions.reason: Carefully remove the plant or inspect the bottom drainage holes. Healthy roots should be firm and light-colored; brown, mushy, or foul-smelling roots indicate root rot.
Allow the top 5 to 8 cm of soil to dry out between waterings, ensure the pot has functional drainage holes, and never let the container sit in standing runoff.

Leaves that have lost almost all chlorophyll cannot photosynthesize effectively and consume plant energy. Removing them with clean shears will improve airflow and allow the plant to focus on healthy foliage.

seasonal_context: During autumn and winter, houseplants require significantly less water due to lower light levels and slower metabolic activity, making them particularly vulnerable to overwatering.
what_to_monitor: Spread of yellowing to remaining green leaves
Browning or darkening mushy spots at the base of petioles or stems
Foul odors emerging from the potting container
limitations: Soil moisture level, drainage condition, and root system are not visible in the photograph.
Pest presence on the undersides of the leaves (such as thrips or spider mites) cannot be ruled out at this resolution.
follow_up_questions: How frequently do you water the plant, and does the pot have drainage holes?
Has the plant recently been exposed to cold air drafts, air conditioning, or moved to a new location?
When was the plant last repotted or fertilized?
